blocks.text: The ape, however, is not a carnivorous animal; Bochart (Hieroz. 1, 3, 36, col. 1036) therefore has the reading קופרים (hedgehog, §. 134) instead of קופין, apes. The reading קופין could, however, be retained if, with regard to the ape, the clearing away of spiders and flies was meant. Voigt (l. c. p. 238) says of apes: “Their natural food is fruit, sweet roots, insects and, above all, eggs. They constantly snatch at flies in order to eat them, and an ape that I once let loose in an uninhabited hall [p. 301] was in an instant busy catching all the spiders from the windows and swallowing them." Thus perhaps in earlier times people may have kept apes in order to catch spiders, flies and other troublesome insects.
The aversion to spiders is very old, cf. Jalkut Schim. part 2, fol. 145, c.: אין בכל השרצים שנואה כשממית.

דבורה, pl. דבורים (Kelim. 16, 7) and דבריאתי (Sota 48b). Beekeeping has always been a lucrative branch of husbandry. The Talmud gives the following method of promoting beekeeping. At the beginning of summer the first brood emerges and flies onto trees; this brood is caught and brought into a new hive. After 9 or 10 days the third generation already leaves this hive, which is in turn caught in a new basket, and which after just as many days produces the fourth generation. These can be obtained 7 to 8 times in one summer, but the later they are, the less they are worth (B. batra 80a).

Only in summer do the bees produce honey; in winter pieces of honeycomb are placed in the basket (hive), on which the bees feed (Sabbat 43b). Their food in summer is water (ibid. 155b) and the juices of flowers, which they seek out in the fields and on the highest mountains (Sota 48b). They are also fond of mustard, which, however, so irritates their palate that they then consume the honey themselves, and heavily, for which reason mustard is not left standing near the beehive (B. batra 18a).

One sees from these statements that the nature of this wonderful insect was not precisely known to the Talmud. As is well known, the whole swarm of bees has only one origin, in that it arises from the eggs of the so-called queen, which after her fertilization lays about 12,000 eggs in the first days. On the twentieth day after the egg was laid, the worker bee (sterile) emerges, on the twenty-fourth day the male (the drone), and the queen (Weisel) is said to appear as early as the sixteenth day (Voigt l. c. 4, p. 273). Of the continually repeated broods, one reckons four per year to a hive; according to the Talmud there would have to be many more.

The swarm of bees is called נחיל של דבורים; it sometimes flies out and settles on a tree, [p. 302] in which case one should not catch the bees individually, but rather saw off the tree, since otherwise the bees could fly away (B. Kama 81b). נחיל is the Arabic نَحْلَة [naḥla].

Conclusion. The beehive is protected both from the heat of the sun and from rain (probably only for the sake of the honey; but, if it is fastened with clay, from the rain for its own sake) by a cover stretched over it (Sabbat 43b). The beehive, which is called כוורת (Kelim 22, 10), was made of straw or of reed (Oholoth 8, 1) and fastened to the ground with clay or nails (Uxin 3, 10). When one wished to take the honeycombs (חליות דבש) out of the hive, the bees were first driven away by burning cattle dung, the smoke of which the bees cannot bear (§. 30), and so they withdraw (Kelim 16, 7). From the honeycombs the honey was obtained (Uxin 3, 11). One takes 10, indeed 20, such combs from a hive (B. batra 80a). Two of them are left in the hive for the winter as food for the bees (ibid.). When the hive is full, the honey flows out of it, and this honey mixed with wax is used especially for medicinal purposes (Sabbat 110b). Honey is usually yellow, sometimes also white (Gittin 69a). Swindlers adulterate it with water (Sota 48b); such adulterated honey is called דבש הזיפין; if it is mixed with flour, yet such that the honey still remains liquid and thin, then it is called דבש הצפחת (Machschirin 5, 9). In ritual respects honey is regarded as a beverage (ibid. 6, 4*). Wax is called שעוה, explained more precisely by קירותא (Κηρὸς [Kēros]) (Sabbat 20b), and קירה (Cera, Jebamoth 102a). Spoiled honey was smeared on the sore (איישרא, ichorous) hump of the camel (B. mez. 38b); it is also given spoiled honey to eat (Sabbat 154b).
The bee dies as soon as it has stung someone (Rabba Bamidbar fol. 269a), because it thereby loses its sting.

גוין usually stands next to צירעין (hornets), but is explained by Raschi as a kind of locust. On Sabbat 106b he says: גוין are a kind of חגב and may be eaten; on Berachoth 7b, he says: גוין and צירעין are kinds of ארבה; already the variation concerning גוין, which are counted now among חגב (§. 384), now among ארבה (§. 373), but even more the evident error of explaining צירעין too as a kind of locust, justifies the assumption that גוין also belong to the order of Hemeroptera and are related to צירעין, the hornets.

Bechoroth l. c. states that by honey without qualification bee honey is understood; this is thus called דבש דבורים (Machschirin 6, 4), or simply דבש for short, but the honey of the hornet is called only דבש הצירעים, and that of wasps only דבש הגוין; thus there can be no question in the remotest sense of locusts.
Sabbat l. c. states: Whoever catches locusts, wasps (גוין), hornets and gnats on the Sabbath is guilty of desecrating the Sabbath.
